entries.title: Cash floods CPS School Board races, with big money groups outraising the Chicago Teachers Union 5 to 1
entries.summary: <p>Back when the idea of an elected school board was still being debated, opponents voiced fears that the powerful Chicago Teachers Union would simply try to buy the elections.</p><p>Yet as Chicago stands on a historic precipice of electing all<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u> 20 members and a citywide president</u></a> on Nov. 3 that’s not how it’s playing out.</p><p>Cash is flooding the election but the bulk<b> </b>so far has come from wealthy, often suburban donors, whose political groups have outraised the CTU five to 1 and outspent the teachers union nearly three to 1, according to an analysis of the most recent campaign finance filings between Oct. 1, 2025 and Oct. 15, 2026.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div style="min-height:311px" id="datawrapper-vis-LhB6K"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LhB6K/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-LhB6K"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LhB6K/full.png" alt="A bar chart with four blue bars of different lengths. The headline reads, “Spending by PACs and super PACs”. The description below reads, “Money that has gone to support or oppose CPS School Board candidates between Oct. 1, 2025 and Oct. 15, 2026”. The bars are sorted from longest to shortest, and each one’s length indicates a dollar amount. At the top, the first bar is nearly double the length of the next. That top bar is labeled “Common Ground Collective” and lists an amount of $3.81 million. Below it is a bar for “Illinois Network of Charter Schools” and an amount of $2.08 million. Next, in a bar that is roughly halved yet again in length from the one before, is “Chicago Teachers Union” with $0.92 million. And below that, slightly shorter, is “Service Employees International Union” with $0.69 million." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Charter school backers and a few prominent billionaires aligned in a shared antipathy for the teachers union have aimed their millions attacking the Chicago Teacher Union’s choice for board president rather than at bolstering any particular candidate, the Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis shows.</p><p>More than a quarter<b> </b>of the $8.1 million total<b> </b>spent on all races so far by these political action committees and the independent expenditure committees, known as super PACs, has targeted a single candidate: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a>.</p><p>The spending to oppose Dominguez is more than four times the amount spent on the top supported candidate, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a>, one of the other two candidates for school board president.</p><p>Biggs, a former CPS principal, has attracted wide-ranging contributions from labor unions other than the CTU, former CPS leaders and investment bankers and CEOs — such as Michael Sacks of GCM Grosvenor and Paul Finnegan of Madison Dearborn Partners.</p><p>Both Biggs and Dominguez have directly raised about $1 million. Defense attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>, who lent himself $500,000, trails in fundraising with no support from special interest groups, unions or PACs — <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/4-takeaways-from-cps-school-board-president-forum" target="_blank" ><u>something he touts</u></a>.</p><p>Arnie Rivera, CPS former chief operating officer<b> </b>who heads a new advocacy group called the Chicago Education Alliance, says the billionaire-funded political groups see the school board races as an opportunity to take down the CTU ahead of the mayoral race in February. Mayor Brandon Johnson remains closely allied with the union, which helped catapult their former organizer to office. Some of the $12.7 million raised by three education-focused political action committees currently spending big will almost certainly be deployed in the mayor’s race.</p><p>“It just becomes a proxy battle on the political side,” Rivera says. “CTU is a huge political group here in the city, and I think you have people who are trying to push back on it. I think that is what it comes down to.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-980000" name="html-embed-module-980000"></a><div style="min-height:611px" id="datawrapper-vis-VDJ4k"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VDJ4k/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-VDJ4k"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VDJ4k/full.png" alt="A chart with five rectangles, all stacked vertically in one column together. A headline reads, “CTU-endorsed candidate for board president is the main target of PAC spending”. The description below it says, “Powerful outside groups have spent about $8.1 million on the school board election so far. More than a quarter has gone to oppose Hilario Dominguez, the Chicago Teachers Union’s pick for president.” The chart’s top two rectangles are different shades of orange, and the bottom three are different shades of gray; a thick black line separates the orange section from the gray section. Above the chart is a label: “Spending by political action committees and Super PACs, in millions of dollars”. The orange rectangles represent spending in opposition of particular candidates, and together they take up about two-fifths of the chart’s overall height. The gray rectangles represent spending in support of particular candidates, and together they take up the other three-fifths or so of the chart’s overall height. The topmost portion of the chart is a brightly colored orange rectangle showing $2.30 million spent opposing Hilario Dominguez; below that is a light orange rectangle showing $0.98 million spent opposing candidates for board member or president other than Dominguez. In the gray section, looking from the other end, there is a small, dark gray rectangle showing $0.58 million spent supporting Dominguez, followed by a similarly sized and lighter gray rectangle showing $0.53 million spent supporting Jessica Biggs. Above those (so in the middle between them and the orange opposition spending) is a large, light gray rectangle showing $3.79 million spent supporting candidates for board member or president other than Dominguez or Biggs." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The latest campaign finance reports from the Illinois State Board of Elections, which were due by midnight Thursday, show an escalation of cash and spending in the last three months, both directly by the campaigns, as well as by outside groups on their behalf.</p><p>The 43 total candidates vying for board seats have directly raised another $4.1 million since the end of June, adding up to $5.9 million in contributions since October 2025. Since August, four candidates have withdrawn. There are also four write-in candidates.</p><p>Candidates just for the board president position account for $3.5 million,<b> </b>including contributions for two who recently dropped out.</p><p>Twenty local district races, 15 of which are contested, split the remaining $2.4 million. Eleven races have accumulated more than $100,000, with one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/1b/" target="_blank" ><u>competitive Northwest Side race in District 1b</u></a> pulling in $292,062 in contributions.</p><p>None of the five district candidates running unopposed are aligned with the CTU. Current school board members <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/che-rhymefest-smith/" target="_blank" ><u>Che “Rhymefest” Smith</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/4b/" target="_blank" ><u>Ellen Rosenfeld</u></a> have raised $100,000 each.</p><p>“I'm open to taking money from anybody,” Smith says, noting that he also has gotten donations from SEIU, the union that represents support staff in CPS. “But I'll tell you one thing that's interesting: they never asked me to vote a certain way. They never have given a policy and said, ‘Push that through.’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div><p></p><h4><b>Big money coming from a new outside group</b></h4><p>The real money in these races is being raised and spent outside the campaigns via a series of political action committees and super PACs. The latter face no limits on how much they can raise or spend, as long as they don’t coordinate with candidates.</p><p>In addition to wealthy charter school supporters who typically amass and spend<b> </b>when school issues are at stake, billionaire Sacks has dropped millions attacking the Chicago Teachers Union candidates via his newly formed Common Ground Collective super PAC.</p><p>That group has spent the most so far, $3.7 million on digital ads and production, about half of it attacking Dominguez, a teacher-turned-CTU deputy political director.</p><p>The group has yet to endorse or fund ads in support of anyone for board president, though Sacks himself gave $400,000 to Biggs earlier this month.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" target="_blank" ><u>A key behind-the-scenes ally</u></a> to former Mayor Rahm Emanuel — who long fought with the CTU — Sacks has given the most money to any of the groups funding the school board elections, $5.5 million as of October 15.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-300000" name="image-300000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Michael Sacks, on the left, with business and civic leader John Rogers, has poured millions into the Chicago School Board race to try to undercut Chicago Teachers Union candidates. He has donated $5.5 million to groups involved with the school board election.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Close on his heels with $3.8 million is Jim Frank, a retired executive from Winnetka<b>, </b>and regular major donor to the Illinois Network of Charter Schools’ political spending groups.</p><p>The INCS Action super PAC has spent $450,000 on a digital ad opposing Dominguez, but only $1,000 supporting one candidate for president who has since dropped out.<b> </b>INCS’ political arms have not made any endorsement for president.</p><p>Outspent by the CTU in 2024, the INCS Action groups have also spent an additional $1.7 million supporting 19 candidates currently in board races,<b> </b>including to candidates who face no opponent.</p><p>Representatives from Common Ground Collective and INCS declined interview requests.</p><p>Dominguez says money isn’t everything.</p><p>“What I'll say is this — that we didn't go from mayoral control to go to billionaire control, right?” Dominguez says. “At no point in this race did we think we were going to be beating billionaires in spending money. One thing that we've seen and we're seeing across the entire country is that organized people beats organized money any day of the week.”</p><h4>Spending big to make a splash </h4><p>The third group aligned in this election against the teachers union is The Urban Center, though its donations and spending are dwarfed by INCS and the Common Ground Collective.</p><p>Juan Rangel, the executive director of the center, which promotes school choice across public and private schools, said if you want to make an impact, you need to spend big money. That requires first educating people that a school board race is happening and explaining what’s at stake.</p><p>“I would hope that people would understand that these school board elections are the most important races on the November ballot, and they will have implications and ramifications to the February mayoral election," Rangel says.</p><p>What’s different about Chicago is that the wealthy billionaires are local, rather than outsiders pushing a conservative agenda, says Jeffrey R. Henig, a professor emeritus at Columbia University's Teachers College, who co-wrote the book, “Outside Money in School Board Elections: The Nationalization of Education Politics.”</p><p>“I'm struck by … the lack of sharp ideological cleavages and the relative absence of the culture war politics that you see in a lot of suburban districts,” he says. For example, no one is pushing book bans.</p><p>He also points out differences between candidates are more subtle than in ones where big national social issues are at play, so “instead of eliminating charter schools in Chicago, it's about how and under what extreme circumstances we might close some schools.”</p><p>Teacher unions usually enjoy a built-in advantage, regardless of money, Henig says. That’s because teachers and parents with a vested interest in what happens in schools are the most likely to show up and actually vote in school board elections.</p><h3>Is CTU spending coming?</h3><p>The CTU ended up outspending everyone else two years ago — $4.3 million via two political action committees, with about half dropping in the last month.</p><p>It’s been slower so far this time in unrolling campaign ads.</p><p>The CTU has disclosed raising about $2.5 million and spent about $2.2 million through its political organization as well as Our Schools PAC, which it funds.</p><p>“What is unusual in spending in a race is spending a tremendous amount of money not for somebody for president but against somebody,” says CTU Pavlyn Jankov, the union’s research director.</p><p>“We’re never going to compete with the billionaires in this race, and our members support our candidates, so we're going to be continuing to put our money into this race because it reflects the values of 30,000 members.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-580000" name="html-embed-module-580000"></a><div style="min-height:353px" id="datawrapper-vis-Gg4nH"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Gg4nH/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Gg4nH"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Gg4nH/full.png" alt="A column chart with four columns, each representing a dollar amount spent in a given month. The headline reads, “How the Chicago Teachers Union rolled out its political spending in 2024”. The description below reads, “Spending by CTU’s political action committee and related PACs on school board races in first school board election, by month”. Below that, the chart shows a column (i.e., a bar stretching vertically) for each month from August through November 2024. The first two (August and September) are much shorter than the remaining two (October and November). August 2024 has an amount of about $164,100. September has an amount of about $301,700. October has an amount (again, much larger than the preceding one) of $1.7 million. November has the slightly smaller amount of $1.6 million." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>More contributions and spending still could come. Like most labor unions, its coffers get replenished through member dues. CTU leaders tried in vain last spring to get members to increase dues, which could have gone toward political spending.</p><p>Robert Bruno, director of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign’ labor education department and author of a book about the 2012 CTU strike, says the union’s resources have been stretched lately, by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/08/17/chicago-teachers-union-illinois-policy-institute-defamation-lawsuit-stacy-davis-gates" target="_blank" ><u>lawsuits</u></a> as well as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/25/ctu-to-cooperate-with-congressional-inquiry-over-financial-audits-chicago-teachers-union" target="_blank" ><u>federal probes</u> — and other elections.</a></p><p>“I can't help but also acknowledge that in addition to this first-ever school board race, there's also the mayoral race, and there's a lot of competition. And that competition involves candidates who have raised a fair amount of money, can raise a lot of money, and obviously, if Mayor Johnson's going to get reelected, he's going to need a very, very highly engaged and supportive Chicago Teachers Union.”</p><p>Plus, he notes, Biggs is no enemy to labor, squarely backed by SEIU.</p><h4>The CTU-SEIU union split</h4><p>Another factor in this election is that the SEIU, the union that represents support staff, has split from its once-close ally, the CTU, after accusing the teachers union of trying to raid some of their members. And they’ve split on most of their candidate endorsements, parting ways on 10 endorsements, including board president. They only overlap on five endorsements</p><p>But Anthony Driver, the chair of a new SEIU-funded PAC Brighter Futures, warned against lumping his union with the other political groups that are anti-CTU.</p><p>“We are not a corporate PAC,” he says. “If anything we are a PAC that operates similarly to the CTU.”</p><p>“We represent low wage workers who are largely erased,” he says, “and it becomes a question of who gets to be heard.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-910000" She is being backed by a wide range of supporters, including SEIU.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Zubaer Khan/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Driver said his members chose to endorse Biggs for president because they believed in her platform — hardly to spite the CTU. That’s the same for individual school board candidates like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/carlos-a-rivas-jr/" target="_blank" ><u>Carlos Rivas Jr.</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/che-rhymefest-smith/" target="_blank" ><u>Che “Rhymefest” Smith</u></a>. “They have stood with us,” Driver says.</p><p>He also pointed out that union PACs have a finite amount of money and so hold their spending until the last few weeks of an election, whereas PACs supported by corporate backers have more resources so can maintain high spending throughout.</p><p>Driver also notes that SEIU is only spending to support candidates, not oppose them.</p><p>Henig said it is not unusual for unions supporting teachers and school district support staff to support different candidates. After all, when it comes to budget cuts, they do not have the same interests.</p><p>Chicago was the outlier, Driver says, which is ”what made us able to build power.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7f0000" name="module-7f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>More CPS School Board coverage</b><br><br>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times have created resources to help voters prepare for this fall’s historic Chicago School Board election.
